data.title: Paramount, Warner Bros. reveal new name
data.description:
(KTLA) – Once the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) merger is finalized, the resulting media empire will fall under a new name.

On Friday morning, David Ellison took to social media to make the announcement.

“What once was the peak is now just the beginning,” he wrote on social platform X. “Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine.”

He added, “Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.”

The name Skydance was taken from Ellison’s film and television production company, Skydance Media. It’s not too surprising, seeing as when he joined his company with Paramount Global and National Amusements in 2025, the latter was renamed Paramount Skydance.

As for the WBD and Paramount merger, Ellison explained that the new name was chosen “for a few important reasons.”

“First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic,” he continued. “Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one.”

Instead, Ellison noted they decided they “wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own” while allowing the two entertainment giants to “remain in the spotlight.”

He also added that Skydance will “honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special,” which means “giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.”

The merger will not only bring together the two Hollywood conglomerates but also HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services, and the television networks CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central and Food Network.

“I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together,” he exclaimed.

It’s been a long journey to get here.

On Tuesday, a California federal judge resolved a lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general, which had opposed the $110 billion merger. Weeks earlier, Paramount reached a settlement in an antitrust lawsuit.

The tentative closing date for the merger is Oct. 6.

Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav is expected to leave his post. He’s reportedly set to receive more than $550 million in stock and cash once the deal closes, including $34.2 million in cash severance payments.

data.title: Grassley calls on Trump administration to ban kratom "NOW"
data.description:
Sen. Chuck Grassley (D-Iowa) on Friday called on the Trump administration to finalize its proposed rule limiting the sale of kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties that can be bought over the counter.

“All Kratom is deadly it should NOT be sold at gas stations/vape stores/ANYWHERE Admin needs 2 put out final 7OH rule NOW Kratom is killing our kids BEWARE of special interest snake oil,” Grassley said on the social media platform X.

Grassley was referring to the Drug Enforcement Administration’s proposed rule published in July that would temporarily schedule any kratom products as Schedule I substances if they contain more than 0.05 percent dry weight of 7-hydroxymitragynine, the opioid-like chemical found in kratom.

While currently not scheduled at the federal level, 11 states have banned it. Kratom is still legal for purchase in Iowa.

The DEA said in July that 7-OH “presents severe risks to public health, including tolerance, dependence and addiction.”

Kratom, or Mitragyna speciosa, originates from Southeast Asia. The plant is not currently scheduled under the Controlled Substances.

The plant is anecdotally touted as being helpful for addicts weaning themselves off opioids, but addiction organizations like American Addiction Centers do not endorse it due to the risk of dependence, a lack of regulation and potential drug interactions.

Overdoses and deaths connected to kratom are rare, though the substance was thrown back in the news last month after two University of Mississippi students were found dead near packages of kratom. It is currently unclear whether kratom was linked to their deaths, though two individuals have been charged for selling kratom in connection to the deaths.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in March published a report finding that between 2015 and 2025, kratom-related exposure reports rose by 1,200 percent.

data.title: Justice Department sues Maryland over federal agent mask ban
data.description:
The Justice Department sued Maryland on Thursday over a new law barring federal law enforcement officers from wearing masks and requiring them to identify themselves while working in the Old Line State.

The complaint, filed the same day the law took effect, argues that Maryland and two of its largest counties are illegally attempting to regulate federal officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, violating the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause.

The new state law prohibits federal, state and local law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings while on duty, with exceptions for certain operations and protective equipment.

It also requires officers to display identification on the outermost layer of their clothing and, when asked, verbally identify themselves.

Officers who violate either requirement can face civil fines of up to $1,500, according to the complaint.

The Justice Department is challenging similar restrictions in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. Prince George’s County’s law carries steeper penalties, allowing officers who violate its requirements to face a misdemeanor charge, up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $5,000.

“The Federal Government, not state and local governments, gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said Thursday.

The department argued masks and limits on displaying officers’ personal identities can protect federal agents from harassment and doxing, and prevent suspects from identifying officers involved in future enforcement operations.

The complaint cites several incidents involving federal officers in Maryland, including an August case in which a Baltimore-area deportation officer and the officer’s spouse were doxed online.

The administration made clear in the complaint that it does not intend to follow the restrictions.

“Federal law enforcement agents and officers cannot and will not comply with the Challenged Laws, which are unconstitutional and recklessly disregard officer safety, public safety, and federal operational needs,” DOJ attorneys write.

data.title: NASA's dexterous humanoid robots built to assist humans on the moon
data.description:
(NewsNation) — At NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, the 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team, is working on new machines to join crews on future lunar missions.

These robots, however, are not just built for repetitive tasks. Their objective is to act as a hands-on support team for the crew while on the moon.

“It’s really about the human elements — either working in environments designed for humans or working alongside humans. That’s our niche,” said Shaun Azimi, Dexterous Robotics Team lead. “We’re uniquely positioned to bring in folks who are designing the human environments.”

The team’s past work includes humanoids such as Robonaut 2, which spent seven years working on the International Space Station, and Valkyrie, NASA’s first bipedal humanoid. These projects gave the team experience with electronics, mechanics, mobility and dexterity.

Applications for the new humanoids also extend to future missions to Mars. Ahead of a crewed mission to the Red Planet, the Dexterous Robotics Team is set to work with other agencies in giving the public a voice on technology ideas for crewed exploration.

The humanoids will work alongside the human crew as assistants on missions to “enhance a crew’s performance and productivity while reducing risk and expanding the capabilities for space exploration” NASA said, with “a focus on robots that can complete tasks humans do with their hands.” 

“Our team is not trying to replace human explorers with robots but instead make human exploration safer and more sustainable by developing highly capable, reliable, and trustworthy robots to work in extreme environments,” Azimi continued.

He added, “If we can send more capable robots, we can reduce the risk and make people more effective in doing the things that people do best.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump brings red state blitz to Alabama; Vance plans Alaska campaign trip
data.description:
President Trump will hold a midterm rally in Mobile, Ala., Friday evening after making similar appearances in Oklahoma and Texas just the day prior.

It’s the latest stop in Trump’s multiday campaign blitz as Republicans are locked in close races ahead of November’s midterms — and both the president’s and his party’s approval ratings have slid. He is set to speak in Mobile, split between two congressional districts that Decision Desk HQ projects will lean in the GOP’s favor, at 7 p.m. EDT.

On Friday, the Republican National Committee announced Vice President Vance would head Monday to Fairbanks, Alaska, on a campaign swing. Alaska Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R) is locked in a tough reelection fight with former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and Democrat Dan J. Sullivan.

As diesel prices soar, Trump announced Friday that Europe will release diesel from its stocks.

The September jobs report out Friday morning revealed the economy added 29,000 jobs — far fewer than expected — and the unemployment rate nudged up to 4.2 percent.

Late Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor in the Cornell sexual assault case. Hochul stopped short on Friday of calling for the resignations of the president of Cornell University or the local prosecutor, though she called the school’s handling of the incident “a failure.”

Follow live below.

data.title: Another former GOP governor backs Hamilton over Marshall for Kansas Senate
data.description:
Former Kansas Gov. Mike Hayden (R) became the second former GOP governor to support Democrat Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in November’s Kansas Senate race. 

Hayden, who served from 1987 to 1991, published an op-ed in the Wichita Eagle Friday endorsing Hamilton for a seat that has not been held by a Democrat for nearly a century. He believes Hamilton will press for relief, real solutions and will listen to constituents.

“I ran for office for the first time when I was only 28 years old because I felt the person representing my community in the legislature was failing to fight for the needs of our state,” Hayden said. “Today, I am endorsing Adam Hamilton for the U.S. Senate for the same reasons.”

Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) also endorsed Hamilton last month over his party’s nominee. He said Marshall had “turned his back” on Kansas, and that Hamilton knows how to “disagree without being disagreeable.” 

The Kansas Senate race is likely to be won by Marshall, according to a prediction by Decision Desk HQ, but is seen as a potentially competitive seat in an election predicted to favor Democrats.

An Emerson College poll taken in September had Hamilton leading within the margin of error, indicating a tight race in the deep red state. 

Hamilton said in a post to the social media platform X that he is honored to have the former governor’s support.

He noted that Hayden has worked “tirelessly” for the people of Kansas and practiced the kind of leadership needed to make a difference. 

“He knows how to put party and politics aside to deliver for working families, and I am so honored to have him by my side as I strive to do the same,” Hamilton wrote.

data.title: Vance set to rally in Alaska as battleground Senate race tightens
data.description:
Vice President Vance is headed to Alaska for a midterm rally against the backdrop of the red state’s highly competitive Senate race.

The Trump 47 Committee, a joint fundraising group connected to President Trump’s Save America PAC and the Republican National Committee (RNC), will host the Monday rally in Fairbanks, the RNC announced Friday. 

With a little more than a month until Election Day, Trump and Vance are blitzing through red states — raising eyebrows as the midterm outlook looks increasingly bleak for the GOP. 

The president is headed to Nebraska on Monday after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week. Vance was in Kansas last month and stumped this week in Florida. 

Asked on Wednesday whether the red state tour signals trouble for the GOP, Trump did not answer directly.

“We have the best economy anywhere in the world,” he said. “There’s no economy like this economy. The only thing we don’t have is good public relations. We don’t seem to be able to get the word across.”

In Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is locked in a neck-and-neck race with Democrat Mary Peltola, who lost the state’s at-large House seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich in 2024. Her moderate, Alaska-first bid has fueled Democrats’ hopes of flipping the seat in a state that’s sided with Trump in each of his three presidential races. 

The Hill has reached out to Sullivan’s campaign for comment.

Alaska has elected a Democrat to the Senate just once in the last 50 years, but the Cook Political Report rates this year’s race as a toss-up. Decision Desk HQ gives Peltola a 60 percent chance of flipping the seat.

data.title: Progressives unveil legislation cracking down on Flock cameras
data.description:
Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) unveiled legislation on Friday to ban federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers.

The bill, titled the Ban Flock Act, would both prohibit federal agencies from ALPR usages and pause federal grant funding to state and local governments with ALPR contracts. It would also allow Americans to sue the federal government for use of ALPRs.

“Going to the doctor? Flock knows. Dropping your kid off at school? Flock is tracking you. Flock is always watching. We cannot allow America to become a surveillance state where a handful of AI oligarchs profit by giving the government the power to track our every movement,” Sanders said.

While there are various ALPR firms across the nation, Flock drew particular backlash this year for its network of more than 120,000 cameras across the country.

Flock’s plate readers not only record license plate numbers, but specific details about a car to create what the company calls a “vehicle signature.” These details include the make, model and color of the car along with unique features like bumper stickers, decals and accessories.

While privacy concerns have long been raised over Flock’s technology, the company’s use of artificial intelligence and a series of recent news reports on law enforcement misusing Flock or other ALPRs sounded the alarm on Capitol Hill.

Other lawmakers are pursuing efforts to quell the concerns.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled a bill last month called The Flock-Off Act, which would block any attempt to purchase, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities and localities. While the bill title references Flock, it would not be the only company impacted.

Republican Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.) led the first Congressional hearing last month on AI-powered surveillance camera manufacturers as part of an investigation into Flock.

Senators heard from lawyers, a sheriff, a cybersecurity engineer and a driver who was wrongfully accused of a crime as result of the technology. Hawley pointed out he asked the CEO of Flock, along with Axon Enterprise, Motorola and Verkada to testify, though none attended.

Weeks earlier, Flock touted a series of policy changes in a letter to Hawley.

Flock’s chief legal officer, Dan Haley, aid Flock does not believe “Americans’ privacy should depend on one vendor’s good judgement, its current leadership or its commercial incentives.”

The company did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on Friday.

Updated at 1:36 p.m. EDT.

data.title: Tony Romo, CBS part ways after DUI arrest
data.description:
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and television analyst Tony Romo and CBS have parted ways after the commentator was arrested on a drunken driving charge earlier this year.

Romo was placed on leave by the network following an arrest on suspicion of drunken driving in July, body camera footage of which was widely circulated on social media.

Footage showed Romo taking sobriety tests and talking with police officers about his history of head injuries.

“CBS Sports and Tony Romo have mutually agreed to part ways,” CBS said in a statement on Friday, according to the Athletic, which noted he had four years and more than $70 million remaining on a 10-year contract worth $180 million he signed in 2020.

After his arrest, Romo announced he would seek treatment for substance abuse and indicated it was his intention to return to the broadcast booth.

“I’m going to use this time to take a break, something I’ve never done before, and focus on my health and my family before moving on to my next opportunity,” he said in a statement shared with the outlet on Friday. “I am grateful for my time with CBS Sports and for the continued support of my family and friends, as well as the NFL community and fans.”

Romo is one of the most recognizable sports media personalities in the country and has called major NFL matchups along with longtime sportscaster Jim Nantz for CBS, including three Super Bowls.

data.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board knocks Hegseth's 'weirdos' line in speech
data.description:
The Wall Street Journal’s conservative editorial board on Friday criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fiery comment during a Wednesday speech to active-duty officers that he wants “warriors” not “weirdos” in the military.

While the opinion piece praised new initiatives introduced by the secretary during this address, including the development of autonomous warfare technology and partnering with universities for officer recruitment, the board expressed concern that Hegseth’s “gratuitous potshots” could negatively impact recruitment efforts. 

“Alas, Mr. Hegseth couldn’t resist his usual polarizing attack routine against all and sundry, and he even accused the press of ‘treason’ for publishing what’s leaking out of the secretary’s shop,” the board wrote. 

“The most remembered line of the speech will be Mr. Hegseth’s declaration that the U.S. military no longer abides ‘beardos’ or ‘weirdos,’” the opinion continued. “As a practical matter, has he met anyone in defense technology lately?”

During his Wednesday speech, Hegseth revived culture-war grievances and declared the Pentagon is “no longer the woke department or the weak department.”

“Simple translation of that: No fatties, no t——, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth continued, using a pejorative term for transgender individuals. 

Alyssa Farah Griffin, a co-host of “The View” and former special assistant to President Trump, said during a Friday show she thought Hegseth’s comment was “a parody” when she first saw it posted online.

“We are the greatest fighting force in the history of mankind,” Griffin said. “We’re not weak, we’re not incapable and I don’t know where he’s hearing this from.”

Griffin called the speech “bizarre” and referenced a new Republican-led effort to remove Hegseth from his role. Last month, GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) introduced an impeachment resolution against the secretary, citing the U.S.’s ongoing military operations against Iran. 

Some Republican lawmakers, including Massie, have become increasingly more outspoken against these operations as the conflict stretches into an eighth month. The House has passed three Iran war powers resolutions with the support of several Republicans, and the Senate approved a similar measure in June.
